# Adoption and Productivity {#sec-adoption-productivity}

A model's capability describes what it can do on a task; productivity is a
measured change in accepted work, the output that passes the organization's own
acceptance rule. The two can diverge. A model can draft faster while making a
reviewer slower, raise one person's output while congesting a shared queue, or
improve a benchmark without changing anything an organization ships. Evaluating
adoption therefore needs a counterfactual, an estimate of what the same eligible
work would have cost and produced under the policy the tool replaces.

@sec-market-structure asked whether a buyer has credible alternatives. This
chapter asks how to measure whether using one of them changes the organization's
work, and by how much. A defensible claim names the accepted unit of work, task
population, worker population, workflow, tool version, review policy, and time
window. Change any one of those fields and the old productivity estimate may no
longer apply.

## Freeze the unit before measuring the tool

Start with a completed workflow unit, not a job title or a model call. A support
unit might be a ticket accepted as resolved after a fixed return window. A
software unit might be a merged change that passes review, tests, and a delayed
defect window. A policy unit might be an adjudicated memo whose claims satisfy a
locked rubric. Attempts that are abandoned, escalated, or rejected stay in the
denominator.

The task-level unit also separates this measurement from occupational exposure
studies, which estimate where language models could reduce task time at
unchanged quality; they do not measure adoption, achieved productivity, job
displacement, or return on investment [@eloundou2024gpts]. Jobs combine many
tasks with coordination, accountability, and work that remains outside the tool.
Aggregate only after the workflow units are measured.

Before the pilot begins, record and freeze the following fields:

| Field | What must be frozen | Why it changes the estimate |
|---|---|---|
| Eligible unit | trigger, required inputs, completion state, exclusions | prevents easy work or abandoned work from silently leaving the denominator |
| Population | task families, workers or teams, experience strata, locations | bounds who and what the estimate describes |
| Treatment | model, interface, retrieval, prompt library, tools, training | makes “AI access” a reproducible intervention |
| Review policy | reviewer role, rubric, escalation, defect window | includes the labor and quality boundary around generation |
| Baseline | current workflow, staffing, software, and service levels | identifies the actual counterfactual |
| Horizon | onboarding, stabilization, and steady-state periods | separates learning from a short novelty effect |

Productivity has more than one valid measure [@oecd2001productivity], so the
decision should rest on a set of metrics: accepted throughput, active labor
time, end-to-end cycle time, first-pass quality, review time, rework,
escalation, severity-weighted defects, incidents, customer outcomes, and worker
experience. A pilot compares arms, each arm being the group of units assigned
to one condition. For each arm $z$, three useful summaries are

$$
P_z = \frac{A_z}{H_z},
\qquad
F_z = \frac{A_z^{(1)}}{N_z},
\qquad
D_z = \frac{\sum_{s=1}^{S} w_s n_{zs}}{N_z}.
$$

Here, $z=0$ denotes the baseline arm and $z=1$ the assisted arm. $P_z$ is
accepted throughput; $A_z$ is the number of accepted units; and $H_z$ is total
paid labor hours, including generation, checking, correction, escalation, and
coordination. $F_z$ is first-pass yield, where $A_z^{(1)}$ counts units accepted
without correction and $N_z$ counts every assigned eligible unit. $D_z$ is the
severity-weighted defect rate; $s$ indexes one of $S$ predeclared severity
classes, $w_s$ is its fixed weight, and $n_{zs}$ is the number of class-$s$
defects in arm $z$. Report raw defect counts beside $D_z$ so a chosen weight
cannot hide harm.

Prompt count, tokens generated, logins, and satisfaction can help explain a
mechanism, but they are not productivity measures, and neither is faster
completion if acceptance quality, rework, or delayed defects deteriorate.

## Estimate the effect of access

When feasible, randomly assign access within prespecified strata, subgroups
such as task family, baseline output, and worker experience, each randomized
separately. Here, $i$ indexes the unit of
randomization, $Z_i=1$ indicates assignment to access, $Z_i=0$ indicates
assignment to the baseline, and $Y_i$ is the locked primary outcome for that
unit. The primary estimate compares outcomes by assignment, whether or not an
assigned unit used the tool. With $n_1$ assisted assignments and $n_0$ baseline
assignments, this sample intent-to-treat effect is

$$
\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ITT}}
= \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i:Z_i=1}Y_i
- \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i:Z_i=0}Y_i.
$$

This estimate measures the policy effect of offering this tool under these
conditions, so it retains people who were assigned access but did not use it.
Actual use is a post-assignment choice. Comparing voluntary users with nonusers
confounds the tool with motivation, task selection, and expected benefit;
calling that difference causal creates selection bias.

Assignment and use diverge when some assigned units never use the tool, which is
called noncompliance. The simplest report is take-up, the share of assigned
units that do use it. A further estimate treats random assignment as a source of
variation in use that is unrelated to motivation. Under the required
instrumental-variable assumptions, it gives a complier effect, the effect on
units that use the tool when assigned and would not use it otherwise. That is
not the average effect for every user [@angrist1996identification].

The cell below simulates 2,000 such pilots of 400 units each. Motivation, which
the analyst never observes, raises both output and the chance of using the tool,
and the tool helps motivated users more. Access is randomized, and the baseline
arm has none. For each pilot the cell computes three estimates: users against
everyone else, the intent-to-treat difference by assignment, and the Wald ratio,
the intent-to-treat effect divided by the difference in take-up, which estimates
the complier effect. It asserts that the intent-to-treat and Wald estimates
center on their true values while the user comparison overstates the effect
several times over. The Wald estimate is also visibly noisier, the price of
dividing by take-up. Change `sel`, how strongly motivation raises output on its
own: the user comparison moves with it, and the two randomized estimates do not.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, reps = 400, 2000  # units per experiment, simulated experiments
sel = 0.8  # how strongly motivation raises output on its own (outcome in standard deviations)
m = rng.normal(size=(reps, n))  # motivation, never observed by the analyst
Z = rng.random((reps, n)) < 0.5  # random assignment of access
complier = m + rng.normal(size=(reps, n)) > -0.3  # would use the tool if given access
use = Z & complier  # one-sided noncompliance: the baseline arm has no access
effect = 0.2 + 0.15 * m  # the tool helps motivated users more
Y = sel * m + effect * use + rng.normal(size=(reps, n))

mean = lambda y, mask: (y * mask).sum(1) / mask.sum(1)
naive = mean(Y, use) - mean(Y, ~use)  # users against everyone else
itt = mean(Y, Z) - mean(Y, ~Z)  # by assignment, whether or not the tool was used
wald = itt / (mean(use, Z) - mean(use, ~Z))  # ITT divided by the difference in take-up
true_itt = (effect * complier).mean()  # the policy effect of offering access
true_cace = effect[complier].mean()  # the average effect among compliers
assert abs(itt.mean() - true_itt) < 0.01 and abs(wald.mean() - true_cace) < 0.01
assert naive.mean() - true_cace > 0.3  # selection makes the user comparison look far better

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
bins = np.linspace(-0.3, 1.3, 65)
for est, c, name in [(itt, "#5b8def", "intent-to-treat"), (wald, "#3dbd8a", "complier effect (Wald)"),
                     (naive, "#ff7a66", "users vs. nonusers")]:
    ax.hist(est, bins=bins, color=c, alpha=0.6, label=f"{name}: mean {est.mean():.2f}")
for v, name in [(true_itt, "true ITT"), (true_cace, "true complier effect")]:
    ax.axvline(v, color="0.55", ls=":", lw=1.2); ax.text(v, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.97, f" {name}", fontsize=7, rotation=90, va="top")
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("estimated effect (standard deviations of output)")
ax.set_title(f"{reps} simulated pilots of {n} units, {mean(use, Z).mean():.0%} take-up", fontsize=10)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right"); plt.show()
```
::::

The unit of randomization must match the interference boundary, the group
within which one unit's treatment can change another unit's outcome. If
colleagues share a queue, templates, reviewers, or meeting load, individual
treatment can spill over into the control arm. Cluster-randomize, assigning
whole teams or workflows instead of individuals, when those interactions are
material, and analyze at that level. A network design, or a saturation design
that varies the treated share across clusters, is needed when direct and
spillover effects are separate decisions of interest
[@hudgens2008interference].

Predeclare a small number of useful strata, such as task family, experience,
error severity, and workflow maturity. Report effect sizes, uncertainty
intervals, and subgroup counts. “Significant here but not there” is not proof
that two subgroup effects differ. Keep the original random assignment through
onboarding and learning periods, and version every change to the model, interface,
prompt library, staffing, and task mix.

## Put value and cost in the same ledger

Operational metrics should be reported separately until the organization has a
defensible rule for converting them into money. When a financial decision is
required, compare both arms over one accounting horizon $H$:

$$
NB_H
= (R_1-R_0)
+ (C_0-C_1)
- C_{\mathrm{fixed}}
- \mathbb{E}[L_1-L_0].
$$

$NB_H$ is incremental net benefit over horizon $H$. $R_z$ is realized revenue or
contribution value in arm $z$; $C_z$ is observed variable operating cost,
including labor, model, review, rework, escalation, and coordination; and
$C_{\mathrm{fixed}}$ is incremental integration, security, legal, procurement,
and training cost. $L_z$ is loss from errors and incidents, so
$\mathbb{E}[L_1-L_0]$ is the change in expected loss. Every term uses the same
currency and accounting horizon. Arm 0 is the baseline arm and arm 1 the assisted
arm.

Avoid two common accounting errors. First, an hour saved is capacity, not cash,
unless the organization can redeploy it, avoid hiring, increase accepted output,
or reduce paid hours. State that conversion rule. Second, do not count a quality
improvement once as revenue and again as avoided rework. If quality or a rare
catastrophic loss cannot be credibly priced, keep it as a separate guardrail and
stress scenario.

For a steady-state unit-cost decision, $C_{\mathrm{fixed}}/N_H$ is the amortized
fixed cost per accepted unit, where $N_H$ is planned accepted volume over $H$.
Keep observed pilot cost separate from forecast volume. Report an uncertainty
interval for $NB_H$ and sensitivity to labor value, volume, incident probability,
and the defect window instead of a single point estimate of return.

@fig-adoption-ledger computes this ledger from the assumptions a pilot must
state, in illustrative dollars for a hypothetical high-volume workflow, not
evidence or a forecast. It shows which assumptions can reverse the decision. A real pilot must populate the ledger from the same accounting period
in both arms.

```{figure}
//| label: fig-adoption-ledger
//| fig-cap: "The chapter's ledger $NB_H = (R_1-R_0) + (C_0-C_1) - C_{\mathrm{fixed}} - \mathbb{E}[L_1-L_0]$ computed from stated assumptions, with illustrative values for a hypothetical workflow, not measured productivity. Saved paid time becomes cash only at the conversion share $\kappa$; the hatched remainder is freed capacity and is not counted, while added time is charged in full. Delayed defects are counted only inside the defect window. The whisker is $NB_H$ at the two ends of the 95% interval on time saved, and the verdict applies the chapter's rule: go only when the lower end clears the hurdle and the incident guardrail passes, and roll back when incidents rise past a predeclared boundary of +5 per 100,000 units. The lower panel moves one assumption at a time by ±30% with the others at base; a range that crosses the hurdle marks an assumption that can reverse the result on its own."
spread: 30
```

## Why a useful tool can look unproductive at first

Economists have described the same gap between capability and measured output
for earlier general-purpose technologies, those adopted across many industries.
The productivity J-curve, named for the dip and later rise in measured
productivity, describes how such a technology can require complementary
investment before its benefits appear in measured output. Organizations first
build intangible capital: new processes, data, training, management routines,
and software. During that period, the investment is costly while its future
services are poorly measured [@brynjolfsson2021productivity].

The same mechanism applies to generative AI. Business-process redesign may
change who drafts, who reviews, which queue owns an exception, and how accepted
work reaches a customer. A separate chat window can improve individual drafting
without changing a shared approval path. The resulting measurement lag does not
by itself show that benefits will arrive later. A pilot should therefore measure
complementary investment, adoption time, and the steady-state workflow instead
of extrapolating from a demonstration.

## Read every empirical result with its boundary

Early studies answer different questions and do not combine into one universal
effect size.

Noy and Zhang randomly assigned 453 college-educated professionals to complete
incentivized, midlevel writing tasks with or without ChatGPT. Access reduced
completion time by 40 percent and raised output quality by 18 percent on those
short tasks [@noy2023experimental]. The experiment establishes an effect on
those tasks; it does not establish a change in team output, employment, or firm
profit.

Dell'Acqua and colleagues ran a preregistered experiment, one whose hypotheses
and analysis plan were filed before the data were collected, with 758
consultants at one firm. The study used two task bundles: 18 product, analysis,
and writing tasks selected to be inside GPT-4's June 2023 capability boundary,
and a business case containing one deliberately selected task outside it. In
the inside bundle, participants with AI completed 12.2 percent more tasks and
worked 25.1 percent faster, with higher rated quality. On the selected outside
task, the combined AI groups were 19 percentage points less likely to be correct
[@dellacqua2023navigating]. The authors call this pattern a jagged frontier:
tasks that look similar in difficulty can fall on either side of what the model
does well. The contrast holds for that model, those consultants, and those
tasks, and it does not define a permanent frontier for other models, workers,
or workflows.

Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond observed the staggered managerial rollout of a
real-time assistant across 5,172 customer-support agents, three million chats,
and a single firm with contractors. They used a difference-in-differences
design, which compares the change in outcomes for agents who received the
assistant with the change over the same period for agents who had not yet
received it. Their main estimate was a 15 percent increase in resolved issues
per hour, with larger gains for less experienced and lower-skill agents. The
highest-skill group saw little throughput gain and small quality declines on
some measures [@brynjolfsson2023generative]. This is field evidence for that
assistant and setting, not a large randomized estimate across occupations.

Dillon and colleagues randomized integrated tool access among 7,137 workers at
66 opt-in firms. During months four through six, workers assigned access spent
1.4 fewer hours per week in email sessions; the instrumental-variable estimate
for compliers was 2.0 fewer hours. The study detected no significant average
change in meeting time, Word time, completed documents, or several coordination
measures [@dillon2025shifting]. The telemetry measured how workers allocated
their time; it did not measure output quality or organizational return. The
result also shows that faster individual drafting need not change a routine
that several people coordinate.

Becker and colleagues randomized whether 16 developers could use early-2025 tools
on 246 tasks drawn from issues in mature open-source projects they knew well. AI
allowance increased completion time by 19 percent, with a 95 percent interval
from 2 to 39 percent slower, even though participants believed the tools had helped
[@becker2025measuring]. The result concerns short brownfield issues, codebase
experts, and February-to-June 2025 tools. It does not estimate current tools,
greenfield development, long-run code quality, or team throughput.

METR, which ran that trial, began a follow-up in August 2025 with the same
design: developers pre-specified their tasks, each task was randomized to AI
allowed or AI disallowed, and developers logged their time. It enrolled 10
developers from the first study and 47 new ones, paid USD 50 an hour instead of
USD 150. The raw estimates point to speedups: 18 percent less time for
returning developers, with an interval from 38 percent less to 9 percent more,
and 4 percent less for new developers, with an interval from 15 percent less to
9 percent more [@metr2026update]. METR judged these a poor proxy for the
effect. Developers who did not want to work without AI declined to enroll, 30
to 50 percent of surveyed participants withheld tasks they did not want to do
without AI, and time logs were unreliable for developers who ran several agents
at once. Both selections
remove the cases with the largest expected benefit, so METR reads the estimates
as likely lower bounds [@metr2026update]. Randomizing within a worker's own
tasks requires workers who accept the control condition, and as a tool becomes
part of ordinary work fewer of them do, so the control arm stops representing
the work the tool is used for. Some developers also reported choosing different
kinds of tasks with agents and producing different work, such as more tests or
documentation, so a time difference inside the study need not be a difference
in value.

That last problem has a general form. When a tool makes some tasks cheaper,
people move time toward them, including tasks they would not otherwise have
done. METR separates three measures of uplift, its term for a productivity
multiplier: uplift on the old tasks, the work done before the tool was
available; uplift on the new tasks, the work chosen once it was; and uplift in
value, which allows for the reshuffle. When workers allocate their time to
maximize value and know how much each task speeds up, uplift on the old tasks is
at most the uplift in value, which is at most the uplift on the new tasks
[@cunningham2026substitution]. Speed measured on the tasks people now choose to
do with the tool is therefore an upper bound on the gain in value, and speed on
the pre-tool task list is a lower bound. Freezing the eligible unit before a
pilot, as the first section of this chapter requires, fixes which of these
quantities is measured.

```{figure}
//| figure: task-substitution
//| label: fig-adoption-uplift-ordering
//| fig-cap: "Uplift measured three ways for a worker who splits an 8-hour day between documents and pull requests to maximize value, after [@cunningham2026substitution]. The two worked examples are the source's: at $\sigma = 1$ time shares stay fixed and the figure reproduces its +33% and +50%, and its +67%, +124%, and +200%. The table times the pre-tool bundle and the bundle chosen with the tool both ways. Value is a CES function of the task counts with equal weights, and $\sigma$ sets how readily time moves toward the task that became cheaper; other values are illustrative. For every setting, uplift on old tasks ≤ uplift in value ≤ uplift on new tasks."
example: small
```

Two cheaper instruments from METR show the ordering at work. A survey of 349
technical workers from February to April 2026, a convenience sample with a
response rate near 2 percent among emailed invitees, found a median
self-reported change of 1.4 to 2 times in the value of work and 3 times in
speed, the order the argument predicts. METR notes that participants in its early-2025 study overestimated AI's
effect on their task time by 40 percentage points on average
[@becker2026survey]. A transcript analysis took 5,305 Claude Code transcripts
from seven METR staff in January 2026, had a language-model judge estimate how
long each task would take an experienced engineer without AI, and divided that
estimate by the time spent. Its author treats the resulting time-savings
factors, about 1.5 to 13 times, as a soft upper bound: the transcripts contain
only tasks people chose to do with the agent, some of which would not otherwise
have been done, and the judge was checked against 34 labeled tasks
[@deng2026transcripts].

Repository studies measure a third kind of outcome, the public output of
open-source projects. Agarwal, He, and Vasilescu defined adoption as a
repository's first agent-generated pull request and used a staggered
difference-in-differences design, the design described above for the support
rollout, here with adoption dates that differ across repositories and matched
repositories as controls. Commits and lines added rose, mostly in the first
months, only where the agent was the first AI tool observed in the project.
Static-analysis warnings and cognitive complexity, a static measure of how hard
code's control flow is to follow, rose by roughly 18 and 39 percent
respectively and stayed higher [@agarwal2026agents]. Zhang, Jiang, and Koziolek applied the same design
to 11,097 repositories from January 2023 to May 2026 with the Sun and Abraham
estimator, which does not use repositories that have already adopted as controls
for later adopters. The number of human contributors did not change
significantly, newcomers' share of participation fell by 3.7 percentage points,
and review depth rose 5.3 percent, which the authors read as work moving from
writing code to reviewing it [@zhang2026augmentation]. Both studies are
preprints. Their outcomes are output counts and static quality proxies,
repositories chose when to adopt, and the estimates are causal only if adopting
and comparison repositories would have followed parallel trends without
adoption.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

METR has not published results from a redesigned trial, and no randomized trial
of coding agents on real repository work has been published since its
early-2025 study. The evidence added since then is observational or
self-reported: the follow-up's raw estimates, surveys, transcript analyses, and
repository studies [@metr2026update].
:::

Broader outcomes can move less than task behavior. A 2026 revision linking
surveys in Denmark with administrative records found rapid chatbot use and task
reorganization, including new oversight and integration work, but no detectable
average effect on earnings or recorded hours. Its estimates ruled out effects
larger than 2 percent at worker and workplace levels two years after ChatGPT's
launch [@humlum2025still]. The result shows that saved task time, changed work,
hours, earnings, and aggregate productivity are different outcomes, so local
time savings can coexist with no measurable change in the aggregates.

## Separate adoption, usage, capability, and realized value

Usage logs show what kinds of requests a product receives, but not whether an
output was correct, accepted, or useful. Anthropic's initial Economic Index mapped more than four
million Claude conversations in total; its central occupational analysis used
self-selected Free and Pro conversations and excluded enterprise and API traffic.
Software-development and writing requests dominated that product sample, but the
study did not observe the user's job, final output, or productivity
[@anthropic2025index].

GDPval is a capability benchmark built from tasks in 44 knowledge-work
occupations. Each is a one-shot task, answered in a single attempt without
revision, in which a model produces an isolated deliverable from supplied
context. Expert graders
found the strongest 2025 models approaching expert deliverable quality on the
public 220-task gold set [@patwardhan2025gdpval]. The benchmark excludes
iterative client feedback, organizational context, integration, and most human
oversight. Usage logs and GDPval measure different things, and neither
establishes causal productivity or an organizational return.

Adoption surveys supply another layer. A nationally representative U.S. Census
Bureau supplement covering November 2025 through January 2026 found that 18
percent of U.S. firms reported AI use in a business function. Among adopting
firms, 57 percent used it in no more than three functions
[@bonney2026microstructure]. Those self-reports measure adoption and breadth, not
causal output gains; the paper's performance relationships are correlations.

Coding agents, systems that read a repository, edit files, run commands and
tests, and submit changes for review, account for the largest share of agent
activity in the usage data Anthropic has published, measured in tool calls on
its API [@anthropic2026agents]. Software was an early site of agent adoption
for a reason this chapter has already used: a code change can be run, tested,
and reviewed before it merges, so the work has an acceptance rule before any
agent arrives. Anthropic's study of agent use makes
the same observation and expects slower adoption in domains where checking an
output takes the same expertise as producing it [@anthropic2026agents].

Coding-agent adoption is published in several units, each with its own
numerator and denominator: seats or active users of a product that also has
features without an agent; revenue run-rate; request, tool-call, or token
volume; the share of a platform's pull requests that involve an agent; and the
share of merged lines attributed to a model. Each measures the reach or volume
of use. None measures accepted work, the quality of what was accepted, or what
the same people would have produced without the tool. A pull request that
involves an agent can still be rejected, reverted, or rewritten by a person, and
a count of merged lines grows with verbosity as well as with finished work. A
figure whose numerator is undefined cannot be compared across platforms or over
time; Microsoft, for example, reported the share of GitHub pull requests that
involve an agent without defining involvement [@microsoft2026fy26q4].
@sec-agents-practice lists the current figures. In this chapter's pilot terms,
they resemble take-up measured without any assignment: they describe exposure
to the tool, an input to an effect estimate rather than a substitute for one.

An aggregate share can also hide concentration. A descriptive study of 25,264
agent-generated pull requests in 2,361 popular GitHub repositories found that
the median repository received one to two of them in a three-month window, that
intensive use was concentrated in a small subset of projects, and that one
person usually reviewed or modified each agent contribution [@raida2026early].

The developers of coding agents publish the same kinds of measures for their own
staff: the share of merged code attributed to a model, lines merged per
engineer, staff estimates of their own output multiple, and the share of
research work that a model leads, rated by the developer's own model acting as
a judge. These figures describe the work that produces the next model, and
@sec-capability-horizon examines what they can show about the rate of AI
research. As productivity evidence they carry the limits of any adoption or
output measure and two more: the party whose products they describe chooses the
definitions, and the underlying logs are private. The developers publish
caveats with them, and a citation should carry the caveat with the number.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

- Anthropic reported on 18 February 2026 that software engineering accounted
  for nearly 50 percent of tool calls on its public API, with no other domain
  above a few percent. The sample of 998,481 tool calls is drawn per call, so
  workflows with many sequential calls, such as repeated file edits, weigh more
  than their share of deployments [@anthropic2026agents].
- Anthropic reports that as of May 2026 more than 80 percent of the code merged
  into its codebase was authored by Claude, counting lines merged to production
  that its attribution pipeline assigns to Claude, and that in the second quarter of
  2026 its typical engineer merged 8 times as much code per day as in 2024,
  which it calls “almost certainly an overstatement of the true productivity
  gain”. In a March 2026 poll of 130 research staff, the median respondent
  estimated about 4 times as much output with Claude Mythos Preview as without
  any AI; Anthropic expects the true uplift to have been somewhat lower
  [@favaro2026rsi].
- OpenAI reported in July 2026 that over six months the share of its research
  compute used for internal coding inference grew 100-fold and internal agentic
  token use about 22-fold, and stated that these adoption metrics do not
  measure research progress on their own [@openai2026gpt56].
:::

| Evidence | What it can establish | What remains unmeasured |
|---|---|---|
| Capability benchmark | performance under a fixed task and grader | adoption, workflow cost, spillovers, profit |
| Product usage log | requests observed on that product and sample | accepted output, counterfactual, causal effect |
| Adoption survey | reported use and organizational breadth | actual use quality, net benefit, mechanism |
| Platform adoption metric | reach and volume of use under the publisher's definition | accepted output, quality, counterfactual output |
| Controlled task experiment | causal effect for its task, people, and treatment | untested workflows and equilibrium effects |
| Field experiment or rollout | operating effect under a real deployment | generalization beyond its firm, period, and policy |
| Administrative outcome study | downstream hours, earnings, or employment | local quality and process mechanisms without linked logs |

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

The category “AI-assisted work” changes over time. Tool capability changes,
workers learn, task mix shifts, and organizations redesign around successful
uses. A positive average can hide harm in a high-severity task; a null firm-level
effect can coexist with valuable local capacity; and an early slowdown can be an
investment or a failure. The claim must stay attached to its population,
treatment version, outcome, review boundary, and date. Heterogeneity, the
variation of the effect across workers and tasks, is a result to estimate over
predeclared subgroups; invoked after seeing a result, it can explain any
outcome.
:::

## Run an adoption pilot as a decision process

A pilot should end with evidence for a bounded decision, one that applies only
to the work units, population, and treatment version the pilot tested. It runs
in seven steps:

1. **Freeze the unit.** Declare eligible work, the acceptance rule, defect
   window, task strata, worker population, and current baseline.
2. **Register the design.** Lock the unit of randomization, primary outcome,
   minimum worthwhile effect, sample and duration, subgroup plan, missing-data
   rule, interim looks, harm boundaries, and rollback trigger.
3. **Instrument both arms.** Capture assignment, actual use, active labor,
   review, rework, escalation, coordination, model cost, failures, and versioned
   workflow events for every eligible unit.
4. **Apply the acceptance rule.** Use a condition-blind review where feasible,
   preserve failures in the denominator, and wait through the delayed-defect
   window.
5. **Estimate effects.** Report arm totals, take-up, intent-to-treat effects,
   uncertainty intervals, predeclared heterogeneity, spillovers, and learning by
   event time. @sec-statistical-reliability covers the interval estimates and
   stopping rules.
6. **Price the ledger.** Convert only defensible benefits and costs, state the
   capacity-to-cash assumption, retain unpriced quality and safety guardrails,
   and stress rare losses.
7. **Make a bounded decision.** Go only when the lower uncertainty bound clears
   the hurdle and every guardrail passes; iterate when uptake or workflow friction
   prevents a conclusion; stop and roll back at a predeclared harm boundary.

The evidence record should retain the protocol and its amendments, assignment
table, task and worker strata, treatment versions, raw arm totals, missingness,
acceptance decisions, defect observations, cost rules, estimates and intervals,
guardrail outcomes, and final decision. NIST's generative-AI risk profile likewise
connects predeployment testing to documented go/no-go decisions, incident
response, and postdeployment monitoring [@nist2024genai].

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

@sec-market-structure determines whether the pilot has a credible alternative;
@sec-economics supplies model and infrastructure costs; and
@sec-statistical-reliability supplies the interval and stopping rules for the
estimates. The next chapter,
@sec-data-rights-economics, adds the rights and compliance conditions that can
make an otherwise productive workflow unusable. The economic unit remains one
accepted and accountable work result, not one token or one model call.
:::
